Name: dimensional_scaling_probing
Title: Do Scientific Foundation Models Internalize Dimensional Consistency and Scaling Laws?
Short Hypothesis: Many established scientific relationships are power laws or exponential/dimensional laws (Arrhenius kinetics, Boltzmann occupancy, allometric metabolic scaling, Coulomb 1/r, diffraction/lattice scaling, DNA melting Tm dependence). We hypothesize that foundation models which predict such quantities encode the corresponding scaling exponents and dimensional structure geometrically in their representations — i.e., a scalar physical input maps monotonically and log-linearly onto a low-dimensional representational axis whose slope recovers the true scaling exponent — and that whether a model recovers the correct exponent (versus a distorted or absent one) is a sharp, measurable diagnostic of true scientific understanding versus curve-fitting.
Related Work: Valeriani et al. (2023) characterize the intrinsic-dimension geometry of transformer representations but analyze abstract semantic structure, not physical scaling laws. Candido/Rives et al. (2026) show protein LM representation space is 'organized like reductionist biology' qualitatively, but do not test whether quantitative laws (with exponents) are encoded. Existing scientific-model interpretability (SAEs, attention-head probing) tests categorical/structural concepts (binding sites, motifs) rather than continuous quantitative scaling relationships. Our contribution is a novel focus on dimensional analysis and scaling-exponent recovery: instead of asking whether a concept is present, we ask whether the model's internal geometry reproduces the exponent and dimensional form of a known law. This distinguishes correct-mechanism internalization from correct-average prediction and is orthogonal to my prior causal-intervention proposal (which edits activations); here we perform read-only geometric analysis of exponent recovery, which is cheaper and applies even to black-box-ish embedding APIs.
Abstract: A hallmark of genuine scientific understanding is capturing not just directions of effects but their quantitative scaling: metabolic rate scales as mass^{3/4}, reaction rates follow Arrhenius exp(-Ea/kT), Coulomb energy scales as 1/r, and DNA melting temperature scales with GC content and length. We ask a simple question: do foundation models for biology, chemistry, and materials internalize these scaling laws and their dimensional structure in their internal representations, or do they merely fit outputs while distorting the underlying law? We introduce Scaling-Exponent Probing: for a set of established laws, we generate inputs spanning the relevant physical variable over orders of magnitude, extract layer-wise representations, and test whether a low-dimensional representational axis varies log-linearly (for power laws) or linearly-in-transformed-coordinates (for exponential/Arrhenius laws) with the physical variable, recovering the true exponent as the axis slope. We define a Scaling Fidelity Score comparing the model-recovered exponent to the textbook value, plus a dimensional-consistency test checking that dimensionally equivalent variables share a representational axis. We apply this across ~10 laws using open models (ESM-2 for length/GC/thermostability laws, a public chemistry transformer for kinetics/Coulomb, a materials model for lattice/bandgap scaling). We predict a spectrum: some laws are cleanly encoded with near-correct exponents while others are compressed, saturated at distribution edges, or absent — yielding an interpretable, reproducible audit of quantitative scientific understanding and a diagnostic of extrapolation reliability.
Experiments: 1. Law curation: Select ~10 scaling/dimensional laws with known exponents across domains: (a) protein: melting Tm vs. length and GC content (nucleic-acid models), sequence-length vs. representation norm; (b) chemistry: Arrhenius rate vs. 1/T, Coulomb interaction vs. distance (1/r), Hammett log(rate) vs. sigma (linear free-energy); (c) materials: bandgap vs. lattice constant, phonon frequency vs. bond stiffness; (d) biology: allometric metabolic scaling if a suitable model/dataset exists. For each law provide the ground-truth exponent/functional form. 2. Input generation: For each law, construct controlled input series that vary the physical variable across multiple orders of magnitude while holding confounds fixed (e.g., synthetic sequences varying only length; molecule series varying only interatomic distance; temperature-annotated inputs). 3. Representation extraction: For each model layer, obtain pooled representations. 4. Exponent recovery: Fit a low-dimensional (PCA/PLS) representational axis maximally correlated with the transformed physical variable (log for power law, 1/T for Arrhenius); estimate the recovered exponent as the calibrated slope mapping representational axis to the physical quantity, and compare to the true exponent via ratio and log-error. 5. Scaling Fidelity Score: aggregate (i) R^2 of the log-linear/linear fit, (ii) exponent-recovery error, (iii) monotonicity across the full range, (iv) extrapolation collapse point (where linearity breaks). 6. Dimensional-consistency test: check that variables with the same physical dimension (e.g., two length variables) project onto a shared representational subspace (measured by subspace overlap/CKA), whereas dimensionally distinct variables do not. 7. Baselines/controls: compare to (a) shuffled-label null, (b) a randomly initialized model of same architecture, (c) an output-level fit (does the model's prediction head recover the exponent even when internal geometry does not?) to separate 'gets the answer' from 'encodes the law'. 8. Scaling with model size: repeat across ESM-2 8M-650M to test whether exponent fidelity improves with scale. 9. Deliverable: an open benchmark of scaling laws + per-model Scaling Fidelity leaderboard, plus a predicted-vs-actual analysis linking internal exponent distortion to real extrapolation errors on held-out out-of-distribution data.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. A model may output correct predictions via the head while the residual-stream geometry does not linearize the law; we address this explicitly by comparing internal-geometry recovery to output-level recovery, which is itself an informative result. 2. The relevant axis may be nonlinearly encoded; we mitigate with PLS and nonlinear (kernel) probes as robustness checks, reporting when linear recovery fails. 3. Constructing confound-free input series is hard for some laws (e.g., cannot vary temperature without changing tokenization); we restrict to laws where clean series are feasible and flag partial-control cases. 4. Some domains (materials, allometry) may lack suitable open foundation models; we will scope to available public models and drop infeasible laws. 5. Recovered 'exponents' from representation axes require a calibration mapping; we report both calibration-dependent exponent error and calibration-free monotonicity/R^2 metrics so conclusions do not hinge on calibration choices. 6. Findings are model- and law-specific and may not generalize, but this diagnostic specificity is the intended output.
